questions.questionText: Describe the methods adopted by Sir Herbert Hope Risley in classifying Indian populations. What are the criticisms against Risley's classification?
questions.subject: Anthropology
questions.microTopic: Unit 2 - Demographic Profile of India
questions.nanoTopic: Ethnic and linguistic elements in the Indian population and their distribution

answers.answerText:
| **✔ Aspects to Take into Account** | **💡 Structure to Follow** | **❌ Don'ts** | | --- | --- | --- | | • Cover Risley's background - Census Commissioner, The People of India (1908)
• Describe the nasal index method: formula, measurement protocol, seven racial types
• Explain the ideological argument: nasal index inversely correlates with social status
• Cover the specific criticisms: scientific invalidity, colonial ideology, single-criterion problem, observer error
• Cover the broader critique: racial typology as discredited framework | • Introduction: Risley and his method
• The Nasal Index Method
• The Seven Racial Types
• The Ideological Argument
• Criticisms
• Conclusion | • Don't miss the social-status correlation argument - it is Risley's most politically significant claim
• Don't miss that modern genetics has decisively refuted racial typology - include this
• Avoid excessive listing of types
• Don't ignore modern perspective | ## Model Answer **Herbert Hope Risley**, as the Census Commissioner for the 1901 Census and author of *The People of India* (1908), provided the first formal racial classification of the Indian population. His work represents the peak of **Colonial Ethnology**, where biological measurements were used to justify social hierarchies. - **The Nasal Index Method:** Risley's primary tool was **Anthropometry**, specifically the **Nasal Index**. He believed the nose was the most "stable" racial marker, unaffected by climate or occupation. - **The Formula:** Nasal Breadth\ Height*100. - He categorized populations into **Leptorrhine** (narrow noses), **Mesorrhine** (medium), and **Platyrrhine** (broad noses). - Risley famously argued that social status in India was inversely proportional to the width of the nose. He stated that the "average nasal index of a caste is a graduated scale of its social standing." - **The Seven Racial Types:** Risley classified Indians into seven types based on his measurements: - **Turko-Iranian** (e.g., Baloch, Afghan) - **Indo-Aryan** (e.g., Punjab, Rajasthan elites) - **Scytho-Dravidian** (e.g., Marathas) - **Aryo-Dravidian** (e.g., Upper Ganges Valley) - **Mongolo-Dravidian** (e.g., Bengal and Odisha) - **Mongoloid** (e.g., Himalayas and Assam) - **Dravidian** (The "aboriginal" type of South India and Central India) - **Scientific and Ideological Criticisms:** Risley's work faced severe criticism from contemporaries and later scholars: - **Scientific Invalidity:** Critics like **A.C. Haddon** argued that a single trait (nasal index) cannot define a race. Modern biology shows that nasal shape is an adaptation to humidity and temperature, not an indicator of "ancestry." - **Observer Error:** His sampling was small and biased toward higher castes. His measurements were often inconsistent and lacked statistical rigor. - **Colonial Ideology:** Risley used the **"Aryan Invasion Theory"** to claim that higher castes were "foreign" invaders and lower castes were "primitive" natives. This "divide and rule" tactic served to delegitimize Indian national unity. - **The Single-Criterion Problem:** By ignoring other features like skin colour, stature, and head shape (Cephalic Index), he created artificial groupings that did not reflect biological reality. **Modern Perspective and Conclusion** Risley's racial typology has been entirely discredited in present times. Modern population genetics (using DNA markers) has proven that there are no "pure races" in India. Instead, the Indian population is a result of thousands of years of migration and genetic admixture. Risley's significance remains historical; he demonstrated how "science" could be weaponized to solidify the caste system into a rigid, biological reality for administrative control.

questions.questionText: Globalisation, on one hand has provided opportunities and on the other hand thrown challenges to Indian villages." Elucidate.
questions.subject: Anthropology
questions.microTopic: Unit 5 - Indian Village and Socio-Cultural Change
questions.nanoTopic: Impact of globalization on Indian villages

answers.answerText:
| **✔ Aspects to Take into Account** | **💡 Structure to Follow** | **❌ Don'ts** | | --- | --- | --- | | • Define globalisation in the context of Indian villages - market integration, communication, migration, cultural flows
• Cover the opportunities: market access, remittances, information, livelihood diversification (opinion of Scholars)
• Cover the challenges: agrarian crisis, cultural homogenisation, inequality, migration's social costs (opinion of scholars)
• Cover specific dimensions: Green Revolution legacy, mobile phones, rural-urban migration, online markets
• Use specific data and ethnographic examples | • Introduction: Defining Globalisation for Indian Villages
• Opportunities - Economic Integration, Information and Social Empowerment with examples (opinion of Scholars like Dipankar Gupta, Satish Deshpande, Arjun Appadurai)
• Challenges - Agrarian Crisis and Inequality, Cultural and Social with examples (opinion of Scholars like DL Sheth, Dipankar Gupta, Arjun Appadurai)
• Conclusion | • Don't write abstractly - specific examples, data, and dimensions are required
• Don't miss cultural globalisation - not just economic | ### **ANSWER** ### **Introduction** In the rural context, globalisation is not merely the presence of multinational corporations, but the **market integration of agricultural produce, the flow of remittances from migrant labor, and the technological penetration of mobile** telephony. It represents what **David Harvey** calls "time-space compression," where the local peasant is directly linked to the global market. - **Opportunities - Economic Integration and Empowerment:** Globalization has provided new avenues for growth and social fluidity: --- - **Market Integration and Value Chains**: The shift toward high-value crops (grapes, floriculture) for export has benefited farmers in regions like Western Maharashtra. Digital platforms like **e-Choupal** have reduced dependency on middlemen through real-time global price discovery. - **Information and Social Empowerment**: **Arjun Appadurai** highlights the role of "media-scapes." For marginalized castes, the internet serves as a tool for social empowerment, bypassing traditional village hierarchies. **Dipankar Gupta** observes that rural India is no longer just "agricultural"; the diversification into non-farm sectors is a direct result of globalized economic flows. - **Remittance Economy**: As noted by **Satish Deshpande**, migration to urban centres and the Gulf has funnelled capital back into villages. These remittances have allowed rural families to invest in "pucca" houses and private education, fundamentally altering consumption patterns and reducing traditional dependence on the landed elite. - **E-commerce for artisans**: TRIFED's Tribes India platform, Amazon Karigar, and independent platforms have enabled tribal and rural artisans to access global markets - potentially reducing dependence on exploitative intermediaries. - **Challenges - Agrarian Crisis and Inequality**: The benefits are unevenly distributed, leading to what **P. Sainath** describes as the "deepening of the rural-urban divide." - **The Agrarian Crisis**: Withdrawal of state subsidies (under WTO mandates) has exposed farmers to global price fluctuations. Reliance on expensive, patented **BT seeds** and chemical fertilizers has led to a debt trap, resulting in the tragic phenomenon of **farmer suicides**. - **Agricultural distress and suicides**: The 2001–2015 period saw over **300,000 farm suicides across India** - predominantly in cotton-growing areas most exposed to global commodity price volatility and input cost escalation. Vidarbha's Bt cotton farmers represent the tragic human cost of imperfect globalisation. - **Economic Inequality**: Globalisation has disproportionately benefited "large farmers" who have the capital to mechanize. **D.L. Sheth** points out that this has widened the gap between landed elites and landless laborers, leading to the **"proletarianization"** of small peasants. - **Cultural Homogenisation and Social Costs**: **Arjun Appadurai** highlights how global cultural flows can lead to the erosion of traditional knowledge. Furthermore, the "aspiration gap" created by mass media leads to a mass exodus of youth, leaving behind "aging villages" and disrupted family structures. ### **Conclusion** Globalisation in Indian villages is a double-edged sword. It has replaced the "Jajmani" interdependence with a competitive **contractual economy**. While it has broken the shackles of traditional caste isolation, it has replaced them with the pressures of global capitalism. For globalisation to truly benefit rural India, the state must transition from being a mere market facilitator to a robust provider of rural infrastructure and social security.

questions.questionText: Describe briefly the proto-history of Gujarat. Discuss the significance of Gujarat proto-history in international trade.
questions.subject: Anthropology
questions.microTopic: Unit 1 - Evolution of Indian Culture and Palaeo-Anthropology
questions.subTopic: 1.1 Evolution of the Indian Culture and Civilization
questions.nanoTopic: Protohistoric (Indus Civilization)

answers.answerText:
| **✔ Aspects to Take into Account** | **💡 Structure to Follow** | **❌ Don'ts** | | --- | --- | --- | | • Define proto-history - period between prehistory and recorded history, known primarily from archaeology
• Cover Gujarat's proto-historic sequence: Chalcolithic (Ahar-Banas culture), Harappan phase (major Gujarat sites)
• Cover the major Gujarat Harappan sites: Dholavira, Lothal, Rangpur, Rojdi, Surkotada
• Cover the international trade evidence: the Lothal dockyard, bead industry, weights and measures, Gulf connections
• Cover Dholavira's unique features - stadium, signboard, water conservation | • Introduction: Gujarat as a maritime proto-historic hub
• Chalcolithic Foundations
• Mature Harappan Sites in Gujarat
• Dholavira - The Most Important Site
• Lothal - The Maritime Connection
• International Trade Significance
• Conclusion | • Don't write only about Dholavira and Lothal
• Don't write a generic Harappan essay - focus specifically on Gujarat's proto-history | ## Model Answer **Gujarat's proto-history** - the period between the prehistoric Stone Age and the literate era - is primarily defined by its strategic coastal geography, which transformed it into a pivotal gateway for the **Indus Valley Civilization (IVC)**. - **Chalcolithic Foundations:** - Before the rise of urban Harappan centers, Gujarat hosted various Chalcolithic cultures, most notably the **Ahar-Banas culture**. - These early agro-pastoral communities laid the groundwork for sedentary life, utilizing local resources and establishing the initial craft traditions in pottery and copper working that the Harappans later industrialized. - **Major Harappan Sites in Gujarat:** Gujarat contains the highest density of Harappan sites in India, showing a remarkable regional diversity: - **Lothal:** Located near the Gulf of Khambhat, it served as a major industrial centre. - **Surkotada:** Significant for its stone-rubble fortification and disputed evidence of horse remains. - **Rangpur and Rojdi:** These sites provide evidence of the **Late Harappan phase**, showing how the civilization survived and adapted even after the decline of the great urban centres of Sindh. - **Dholavira - The Jewel of Kutch:** Situated on Khadir Bet in the Rann of Kutch, **Dholavira** is one of the most spectacular IVC sites. - **Urban Planning:** It features a unique tripartite division (Citadel, Middle Town, and Lower Town) and extensive use of stone rather than just brick. - **Innovations:** It boasts a massive **stadium**, a ten-character "**signboard**," and an unparalleled system of **water conservation** through rock-cut reservoirs, essential for its arid environment. - **Lothal and the Maritime Connection:** Lothal is synonymous with the Harappan maritime genius. Its most striking feature is the dockyard, a trapezoidal brick structure connected to the Sabarmati river, designed to handle ships during high tides. - **Bead Industry:** Lothal was a global centre for semi-precious stone beads (carnelian, agate). The discovery of a bead-making factory with kilns highlights its industrial scale. - **International Trade Significance:** Gujarat was the lynchpin of IVC's international commerce: - **Gulf Connections:** "Persian Gulf" seals and "Bun-shaped" copper ingots found at Lothal confirm trade with **Dilmun** (Bahrain) and **Magan** (Oman). - **Exports:** Harappan seals and carnelian beads from Gujarat have been excavated in **Mesopotamian** sites like Ur and Kish, where the IVC was known as "Meluhha." - **Standardization:** The use of uniform weights and measures ensured a regulated trade system that stretched thousands of miles across the sea. ### **Conclusion** The proto-history of Gujarat is a testament to early globalization. By leveraging its 1,600 km coastline, Gujarat transitioned from a regional Chalcolithic base to a world-class maritime powerhouse.

questions.questionText: Critically examine 'Indigenisation of Christianity' in India.
questions.subject: Anthropology
questions.microTopic: Unit 3 - Traditional Indian Social System and Caste
questions.subTopic: 3.4 Impact of Religions on Indian society
questions.nanoTopic: Impact of Islam and Christianity

answers.answerText:
| **✔ Aspects to Take into Account** | **💡 Structure to Follow** | **❌ Don'ts** | | --- | --- | --- | | • Define indigenisation of Christianity - the process by which Christianity adapts to Indian cultural contexts
• Cover the historical process: St. Thomas tradition, colonial missionary Christianity, inculturation movement
• Cover specific forms: ashram Christianity, use of Sanskrit in liturgy, Indian musical forms, Indian art by Rober de Nobili
• Cover successful indigenisation examples: Syro-Malabar church, North-East tribal Christianity
• Critical examination: tensions between universal Christianity and local culture, theological controversies | • Introduction: Christianity as both global and local
• What Indigenisation Means
• Historical Phases of Indigenisation (including role of Robert Nobili)
• Forms of Indigenisation in India
• Tensions and Theological Controversies
• Critical Assessment
• Conclusion | • Don't write a straightforward history of Christianity in India - the question is about the indigenisation process specifically
• Don't miss North-East India's tribal Christianity - it is perhaps the most successful example of indigenisation
• Don't avoid the critical dimension - theological, social, and political tensions must be addressed
• Don't miss the ashram Christianity movement - figures like Robert Nobili, Brahmabandhab Upadhyay and Abhishiktananda | ## Model Answer Indigenisation, or **Inculturation**, refers to the process by which Christianity **integrates into the cultural, social, and philosophical** landscape of India. It seeks to strip Christianity of its "Western" casing to express its core message through indigenous symbols, rituals, and thought-forms. - **Historical Phases: From Syrian Origins to Jesuit Adaptation:** Christianity's indigenisation has occurred in distinct waves: - **The Apostolic Phase:** The **St. Thomas (Syro-Malabar) Christians** of Kerala represent the earliest successful indigenisation. They adopted the "Hindu" social identity (caste-like status) while maintaining a Christian faith, famously described as "Hindu in culture, Christian in religion, and Oriental in worship." - **The Jesuit Experiment:** In the 17th century, **Robert de Nobili** adopted the lifestyle of a *Sannyasi* in Madurai. He learned Sanskrit and Tamil, wore saffron robes, and even used a **sacred thread** to present Christianity as a "spiritual completion" of the Vedas rather than a foreign disruption. - **Forms of Indigenisation in India** - **Ashram Christianity:** Movements led by figures like **Brahmabandhab Upadhyay** and later **Abhishiktananda** sought to create Christian "Ashrams" that mirrored Hindu monastic life, emphasizing meditation and simplicity. - **Aesthetics and Liturgy:** Indigenisation is visible in the use of **Sanskrit** in the Catholic liturgy, Indian classical music (bhajans) in worship, and the portrayal of Christ and Mary in Indian artistic styles (e.g., Jesus in a meditative yogic posture). - **Tribal Christianity (North-East):** In states like Nagaland and Mizoram, Christianity has been synthesized with tribal identity. It provided a script for local languages and integrated traditional festivals with Christian holidays, becoming a tool for modern tribal self-assertion. - **Tensions and Theological Controversies:** The process has faced significant criticism from both within and without: - **Universal vs. Local:** Conservative sections within the Church often view indigenization as **Syncretism** - a dilution of the original Gospel. The "Malabar Rites" controversy was a historic example of Rome's discomfort with local adaptations. - **Social Tensions:** Critics from other religious groups sometimes view indigenisation as a "deceptive missionary strategy" (proselytization in disguise). - **The Caste Paradox:** While seeking cultural integration, some churches inadvertently adopted the **caste system**, leading to the marginalization of "Dalit Christians," which contradicts the egalitarian core of the faith. ### **Conclusion** Indigenisation has allowed Christianity to become an "Indian religion" rather than a colonial relic. While theological controversies persist, successful models like the Syro-Malabar church and North-East tribal communities prove that Christianity in India is most resilient when it speaks through the local cultural idiom. True indigenisation, however, remains a work in progress as the Church continues to navigate the thin line between cultural appreciation and religious compromise.

questions.questionText: Write short notes on the following in about 150 words each: Regionalism as an opportunity and threat to national integration
questions.subject: Anthropology
questions.microTopic: Unit 7 - Ethnicity, Unrest, and Political Developments
questions.nanoTopic: Unrest among tribal communities, Regionalism and demand for autonomy

answers.answerText:
| **✔ Aspects to Take into Account** | **💡 Structure to Follow** | **❌ Don'ts** | | --- | --- | --- | | • Define regionalism - political mobilisation around regional identity, language, or cultural distinctiveness
• Cover the opportunities: devolution of power, linguistic federalism, diverse cultural heritage, checks on central overreach
• Cover the threats: separatism, inter-regional economic competition, demands undermining constitutional federalism
• Cover Indian examples: successful regionalism (linguistic states, North-East peace accords), threatening regionalism (secessionist movements)
• Reach a nuanced position | • Introduction: Regionalism Defined
• Regionalism as Opportunity
• Regionalism as Threat
• Indian Case Studies
• Conclusion | • Don't write only negatively - regionalism has produced positive outcomes in Indian democracy
• Don't miss the linguistic reorganisation of states as the key example of positive regionalism
• Don't miss the North-East as the key example of the threat dimension that was partially resolved
• Don't ignore the economic dimensions - inter-regional resource and water disputes are major threats | ## Model Answer Regionalism in India refers to political mobilization based on sub-national identities, such as language, culture, or geography. While often viewed as a centrifugal force, it acts as both a democratic lubricant and a potential fracture point for national integration. - **Regionalism as an Opportunity**: Regionalism can strengthen the democratic fabric by fostering **Linguistic Federalism**. - **Devolution of Power**: It forces the centre to acknowledge local aspirations, leading to better governance through decentralized planning. - **Cultural Preservation**: It protects diverse heritages from being swallowed by a homogenous national identity. - **Democratic Balance**: Regional parties act as a check on "central overreach," ensuring that the Union remains truly federal rather than unitary. - **Regionalism as a Threat**: When regionalism transitions into **Sub-nationalism** or **Secessionism**, it poses a direct threat to the state. - **Separatism**: Radical regionalism can lead to demands for "Sovereign States," undermining the territorial integrity of India. - **Resource Conflicts**: It often manifests as inter-state disputes over river waters (e.g., Cauvery) or **"Sons of the Soil"** movements that target internal migrants, damaging the national labour market and social harmony. - **Economic Disparity**: Competitive regionalism can lead to **"beggar-thy-neighbour"** policies, where states compete for investments at the cost of national economic cohesion. - **Indian Case Studies** - **Successes**: The **Linguistic Reorganisation of States (1956)** successfully channelled regional identities into a stable administrative framework. Similarly, various **North-East Peace Accords** (e.g., Mizo Accord) transformed secessionist movements into mainstream political participation. - **Challenges:** The violent insurgencies in Nagaland or the Khalistan movement of the 1980s represent the destructive potential of regionalism when it rejects the Constitutional framework. ### **Conclusion** Regionalism is not inherently anti-national. It is a natural expression of India's **"Unity in Diversity."** As long as regional aspirations are accommodated through institutional mechanisms like the **Finance Commission** or **Zonal Councils**, regionalism serves as a pillar of a resilient federal democracy. The threat only emerges when the "region" is placed in absolute opposition to the "nation."

questions.questionText: Write short notes on the following in about 150 words each: Issues of tribal agricultural labourers
questions.subject: Anthropology
questions.microTopic: Unit 7 - Exploitation, Unrest, and Marginalized Communities
questions.nanoTopic: Problems of exploitation and deprivation of SCs, STs and OBCs

answers.answerText:
| **✔ Aspects to Take into Account** | **💡 Structure to Follow** | **❌ Don'ts** | | --- | --- | --- | | • Define tribal agricultural labourers - tribal people who have lost land and work as wage labourers in agriculture
• Cover the scale: NSS/PLFS data on tribal landlessness and agricultural labour dependence
• Cover the specific issues: bonded labour, low wages, seasonal unemployment, absence of social security
• Cover the legal framework: Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, MNREGA, minimum wage laws
• Cover the failure of implementation | • Introduction: tribal agricultural labourers as a distinct vulnerable category
• Scale and Distribution
• Specific Issues - Bonded Labour
• Wages, Seasonality, and Social Security
• Legal Framework
• Implementation Gaps
• Conclusion | • Don't write a general essay on tribal problems - focus specifically on agricultural labourers
• Don't ignore the gender dimension - women agricultural labourers face additional discrimination | ## Model Answer The transition of Scheduled Tribes (STs) from "lords of the forest" to landless agricultural labourers represents a process of **proletarianization** driven by land alienation and the erosion of traditional livelihoods. Unlike general agricultural labor, tribal laborers face a unique intersection of ethnic marginalization and economic exploitation. - **Scale and Distribution** - According to NSSO and PLFS data, nearly **45-50%** of the tribal workforce is engaged as agricultural laborers. - This high dependence stems from the loss of ancestral lands to industrialization and mining, pushing tribes into a precarious "wage-earning" existence, particularly in states like Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, and Odisha. - **Core Issues: Bonded Labour and Seasonality** - **Bonded Labour:** Despite the **Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act (1976)**, many tribals remain trapped in debt bondage. Advance payments during lean seasons often lead to intergenerational cycles of forced labour. - **Wages and Seasonality:** Tribal labourers often receive wages below the statutory minimum. The seasonal nature of agriculture leads to chronic **disguised unemployment**, forcing "distress migration" to brick kilns or urban construction sites. - **Gender Dimension:** Tribal women constitute a significant portion of this workforce but face a double burden: they are paid lower wages than men for the same tasks and lack access to maternity benefits or childcare at worksites. - **Legal Framework and Implementation Gaps:** While **MGNREGA** and **Minimum Wages Act** aim to provide a safety net, implementation is hampered by: - **Administrative Apathy:** Delays in wage payments and lack of awareness about legal rights. - **Absence of Social Security:** Most labourers fall under the unorganized sector, lacking provident funds or health insurance. - **Lack of Unionization:** Unlike industrial labour, tribal agricultural laborers are geographically dispersed and lack collective bargaining power. ### **Conclusion** The plight of tribal agricultural laborers is not just a result of poverty, but of **structural displacement**. Without effective land restoration and the strict enforcement of labour laws, they remain "alienated" in their own geography-working the land they once owned for survival rather than sustenance.

questions.questionText: Write short notes on the following in about 150 words each: Major problems of nomadic and semi-nomadic groups
questions.subject: Anthropology
questions.microTopic: Unit 1 - Evolution of Indian Culture and Palaeo-Anthropology
questions.nanoTopic: Survivals and Parallels among communities (hunting, pastoral, peasant, arts and crafts)

answers.answerText:
| **✔ Aspects to Take into Account** | **💡 Structure to Follow** | **❌ Don'ts** | | --- | --- | --- | | • Define nomadic/semi-nomadic groups - communities without fixed residence, moving seasonally or as livelihood requires
• Cover the Indian context: denotified tribes, pastoral nomads, itinerant artisans, seasonal labourers
• Cover the specific problems: no fixed address (legal identity), no land rights, Habitual Offenders Acts continuation, no welfare access
• Cover the National Commission for DNT tribes (Renke Commission) recommendations
• Cover recent government responses | • Introduction: Who Are Nomadic/Semi-Nomadic Groups in India?
• Legal Identity and Documentation
• Habitual Offenders Acts - Colonial Stigma Persists
• No Land, No Welfare Access
• Policy Responses
• Conclusion | • Don't write only about pastoralists - include denotified tribes and itinerant artisan groups
• Don't miss the Habitual Offenders Acts - they are the most legally significant problem
• Don't miss the Renke Commission (2008) - it is the key policy document | ## Model Answer Nomadic and Semi-Nomadic Communities (NSNCs) in India constitute a diverse group including pastoralists (Gujjars, Bakarwals), itinerant artisans (Gadiya Lohars), and Denotified Tribes (DNTs). Despite their vibrant culture, their mobility - once a survival strategy - has become a structural barrier in a modern state designed for sedentary populations. - **Legal Identity and Documentation** - The primary crisis is the **lack of a permanent address**. Without a "fixed residence," these groups struggle to obtain basic identity documents like Aadhaar, Voter IDs, or Ration Cards. - This "invisibility" before the state results in the systemic exclusion from welfare schemes, banking, and the formal electoral process. - **The Colonial Stigma: Habitual Offenders Act** - Many nomadic groups were branded as "born criminals" under the British-era **Criminal Tribes Act (1871)**. Although "denotified" in 1952, the spirit of this law persists through the **Habitual Offenders Acts** enacted by various states. - This leads to constant police harassment, social stigmatization, and the criminalization of their traditional livelihoods. - **Land Rights and Welfare Exclusion** - **Loss of Common Resources:** Encroachment on grazing lands and strict forest laws have squeezed pastoral nomads out of their traditional habitats. - **Education and Healthcare:** Since schools and hospitals are location-bound, nomadic children often drop out, and the elderly lack access to continuous medical care. - **Economic Displacement:** Modern markets have rendered the services of itinerant artisans and entertainers (like snake charmers or street performers) obsolete, pushing them into unskilled manual labor. - **Policy Responses** - The **Renke Commission (2008)** highlighted that nearly 94% of DNTs were landless and advocated for their inclusion under the SC/ST categories to provide reservation benefits. - More recently, the government established the **National Commission for Denotified, Nomadic and Semi-Nomadic Tribes (NCDNT)** and launched the **SEED (Scheme for Economic Empowerment of DNTs)** to provide health insurance, housing, and coaching. ### **Conclusion** The problems of nomadic groups are rooted in a "sedentary bias" of governance. National integration for these communities requires moving beyond "settlement" projects toward "mobile" service delivery that respects their right to movement while guaranteeing their rights as citizens.

questions.questionText: Write short notes on the following in about 150 words each: Role of the Governor in the Fifth Schedule areas
questions.subject: Anthropology

answers.answerText:
| **✔ Aspects to Take into Account** | **💡 Structure to Follow** | **❌ Don'ts** | | --- | --- | --- | | • Define Fifth Schedule areas and their significance (Article 244(1))
    ◦ Cover the Governor's specific powers: power to modify/annul central/state laws, power to direct restrictions on tribal land alienation
    ◦ Cover the annual report requirement to the President
    ◦ Cover the Tribal Advisory Council (TAC) - consultative role; Governor's role in TAC
